rules.N1: Numbers A Form number is an int (i64, or u64 per N2) or a float (finite f64). The type is part of the value and is kept across every boundary: a float with no fractional part stays a float (`10.0` is written `10.0` in canonical JSON, `10` is an int), and `-0.0` keeps its sign (N3 F6). Derivation: encoding must be injective and round-trip, `decode(encode(v)) == v`, because replay rebuilds state from D. Turning `10.0` into `10` at a boundary would decode as an int, changing the static type a later step sees and the bits of later float arithmetic, so no normalization is applied. RCE's static types make the int/float distinction visible to the programmer, and canonical JSON keeps it visible in D.
rules.N10: Absence `none` and a present `()` differ, exactly as the Form's null-versus-absent rule: an option field holding none is present.
rules.N11: Time is the logical clock only: `Tick` events and `after n` in `select`. No construct reads a wall clock.
rules.N2: Integer arithmetic is checked: overflow of the *static type's* range is `trap("overflow: V is outside T")` with V the exact result and T the static type (`i64` for an untyped literal), never a wrap. `/` truncates toward zero (`-7 / 2 = -3`); `%` has the sign of the dividend (`-3 % 2 = -1`). Division or remainder by zero is `trap("division by zero")`. Modular and clamped arithmetic are explicit methods, never the default: `a.wrapping_add(b)`, `wrapping_sub`, `wrapping_mul` give the result modulo 2^N mapped into the static type's range, and `saturating_add`, `saturating_sub`, `saturating_mul` clamp it to the range; neither traps. u64 and usize arithmetic uses the Form ops `uadd usub umul udiv urem` (draft 0.5), which compute the exact result and trap unless it lies in [0, 2^64); a value at or above 2^63 is carried as an unsigned Form int, so `18446744073709551615 - 1` is exact. Lean: `RCE/U64.lean`. `i64.MIN / -1` and `i64.MIN % -1` are `trap("overflow: 9223372036854775808 is outside i64")` (the quotient is out of range; Rust's `checked_rem`). Shifts: `x << n` and `x >> n` with n ≥ bit width or n < 0 are `trap("shift amount out of range")`; `>>` is arithmetic for signed and logical for unsigned types. Bitwise `& | ^ ~` act on the two's-complement representation of the static type.
rules.N3: Floats The rules below are derived from IEEE 754-2019 and from two requirements of the Form: replay must give the same bits on every target (T1), and δ must be total (S1). `tests/float_rules.rs` checks each rule on the interpreter; the parity set carries the vectors of `examples/57_float_vectors.rce` to every CI target. - **F1 Correct rounding.** f64 is IEEE binary64. `+ - * /` and `sqrt` are the standard's basic operations, correctly rounded with roundTiesToEven, the default rounding-direction attribute; so are the conversion of an integer (`as f64`) and of a decimal literal. A correctly rounded operation is a function of its operands' bits alone, so every conforming target gives the same result: this is the only property determinism needs, and no other rounding mode exists in RCE. - **F2 One rounding per operator, in source order.** Float addition and multiplication are not associative and `a * b + c` with one rounding differs from two roundings (vector `MulSub`: `0.1 * 10.0 - 1.0` is `0`, fused it is `5.551115123125783e-17`). Contraction to fused multiply-add, reassociation, excess precision and every other value-changing optimization the standard allows a language to permit are therefore not valid compilations (HC-14). A fused multiply-add is itself correctly rounded, so it may exist only as an explicit named operation; RCE has none yet. Adding one needs a correctly rounded implementation on every runtime (Rust `f64::mul_add`, Java `Math.fma`, exact rational rounding in Python and JavaScript). - **F3 Subnormals are preserved.** Gradual underflow is part of the binary64 format; flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero modes are not IEEE operations and would make `x - y == 0` hold for `x != y`. A host never enables them (HC-13); vectors `Mul(5e-324, 3.0)` and `Mul(2.2250738585072014e-308, 0.5)` detect either mode. - **F4 Non-finite results trap (from totality).** A Form value must have a reflexive equality and a total order (6.2, N5, N6) and must encode as a JSON number for hashing (N1). NaN is unequal to itself under IEEE comparison, and an infinity is not a JSON number and reintroduces NaN through `inf - inf` and `0 * inf`; the largest subset of binary64 closed under these requirements is the finite values. δ is total as a function into values and traps, so an operation whose IEEE result is not finite (the standard's overflow, divideByZero and invalid exceptions) is `trap("non-finite float")`. The alternatives fail a law: admitting NaN under the standard's totalOrder makes `==` disagree with IEEE comparison and needs a canonical NaN for hashing; saturating to the largest finite value is not an IEEE result and breaks `x * 2.0 / 2.0 == x` without a signal. With the trap every value is finite and every result that does not trap is the IEEE result. `x / 0.0` and `sqrt` of a negative number trap. - **F5 NaN payloads are never observable.** By F4 no NaN becomes a value, so its sign, payload and quiet bit cannot reach state, output or a hash; the standard leaves payload propagation to the implementation, which is why this matters. An implementation tests for a non-finite result before any NaN escapes, and the trap text is the same for every NaN. A fabric or target that can produce NaN (GPU, NPU, WASM SIMD) canonicalizes or traps before a value reaches state (HC-13; `wasm_float.rs` rewrites NaN to the canonical positive NaN). - **F6 Signed zero is a distinct state.** `-0.0` arises by the standard's sign rules, which are exact, so every target produces it in the same places (vector `Mul(0.0, -1.0)`). It is observable: `tostr` prints `-0` (f64 and f32 alike, so text round-trips), and the sign decides later results through the same exact rules. The state hash must be injective on observable state, so canonical JSON keeps the sign and a state holding `-0.0` hashes differently from one holding `0.0`; the canonical order (6.1) is totalOrder, so they are distinct map keys. `-0.0 == 0.0` is still true: `==` is IEEE comparison. - **F7 Exception flags are not state.** Inexact and underflow raise nothing (F1 already fixes the result); overflow, divideByZero and invalid are the trap of F4. No program reads a flag. - **F8 Exact operations.** `floor`, `ceil` and `round` are the standard's roundToIntegral operations toward negative, toward positive and ties-away (`(2.5).round()` is `3`, `(-2.5).round()` is `-3`); `abs` clears the sign. `min` and `max` follow N5. None of these rounds. - **F9 Transcendentals are correctly rounded RCE code, or absent.** IEEE 754-2019 recommends but does not require correctly rounded `exp`, `log`, `sin`, `pow` and the like, and platform math libraries differ in the last bit, so no runtime takes one from its platform library and no Form op names one. A transcendental exists only as RCE source in the standard library module `math` (`stdlib/lib/math/math.rce`), built from the operations of F1 to F8 and integers, so every runtime carries the same algorithm and the result is the same bits on every target (vector parity: Rust, Python, JavaScript, Scala). Each function must be correctly rounded by construction: algebraic ones (`cbrt`, `hypot`) compare the exact value with the rounding midpoints in exact arithmetic (TwoSum, Veltkamp/Dekker TwoProduct, Shewchuk expansions; exact ties round to even); transcendental ones use Ziv's strategy over exact integers (the value is bracketed with an explicit error bound and the precision grows until both ends round alike; a transcendental value of a double is never a midpoint), `sin` and `cos` with Payne-Hanek reduction exact for every finite argument. Each is checked bit for bit against MPFR on the CORE-MATH worst cases. Present: `sqrt` (F1), `cbrt`, `hypot`, `exp`, `log`, `log2`, `log10`, `sin`, `cos`; any other (`pow`, `tan`, `atan2`, ...) is absent until it meets the same rule. A result that overflows traps (F4); `log` of x ≤ 0 traps (also `log2`, `log10`). Device versions stay output only or verified (HC-13). Float *text* (the result of `tostr` and of `Show` on a float, `interp::float_text`) is the shortest round-trip digits; decimal notation for 1e-5 ≤ |x| < 1e16, else `d.ddde±N` with `+` on positive exponents (`1e+300`, `1.5e-7`). It is a program-visible value and is never hashed. Canonical JSON (6.1.1) is a different, separately specified byte form: it has one float form, `interp::float_json`, used for hashes and for every trace and log written as JSON, so a trace shows the bytes that were hashed: shortest round-trip digits, decimal with at least one fractional digit for 1e-4 ≤ |x| < 1e16 (`10.0`, `0.0001`), otherwise exponent form without `+` (`1e16`, `1e-5`, `5e-324`), and `-0.0` keeps its sign (`tests/traces.rs` pins these forms). **f32 (draft 0.5).** The Form ops `f32add f32sub f32mul f32div` round both operands to binary32, compute in binary64, and round the result to binary32 (round to nearest even). Binary64 has 53 ≥ 2·24 + 2 significand bits, so by Figueroa's theorem the result equals the correctly rounded binary32 result, and every target (Rust `f32`, Python `struct`, JavaScript `Math.fround`) gives the same bits. A result outside the binary32 range is `trap("non-finite float")`. `x as f32` (Form `tof32`) rounds once. Lean: `RCE/F32.lean`.
rules.N4: Mixed arithmetic does not exist in RCE (both operands of a binary operator have the same static type). `a as f64` converts an integer exactly when |a| ≤ 2^53 and otherwise rounds to nearest even; `x as iN` truncates toward zero and traps if the result is out of range or x is not finite.
rules.N5: min / max compare exactly on integers and by IEEE order on floats (total, since operands are finite); on a tie the receiver is returned.
rules.N6: Equality is structural value equality within one static type; `1 == 1.0` is a type error (the type is part of the value, N1). Float `==` is IEEE comparison, so `-0.0 == 0.0` although the two are distinct states (N3 F6).
rules.N7: Text is a sequence of Unicode scalar values compared by code point, stored as UTF-8. From draft 0.5, `len`, indexing and slicing count UTF-8 bytes (Form `blen`, `bget`, `bslice`): `s[i]` is a `u8`, and a slice whose ends are not character boundaries is `trap("not a char boundary")`. `for c in s` and `chars()` still go by character. Case mapping (`upper`, `lower`) and class tests (`isdigit`, `isalpha`, `isupper`, `islower`) are ASCII-only; other characters are unchanged / false. `strip`, `words` and `toint` treat as whitespace exactly the 25 code points of the White_Space property of Unicode 18.0.0: U+0009 to U+000D, U+0020, U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000 to U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F and U+3000 (`interp::WHITE_SPACE`). `isspace` is ASCII (space, \t, \n, \x0c, \r). Display writes text in double quotes, with U+0000, tab, LF, CR, `"` and `\` as `\0`, `\t`, `\n`, `\r`, `\"` and `\\`, each code point of the *display escape set* as `\u{h}` (h its lower-case hexadecimal digits, without leading zeros), and every other code point as itself. The display escape set is the 911 ranges of code points listed in `spec/data/display-escape.json` (`interp::display_escaped`; the emitter writes the same ranges into each emitted runtime): the control characters, the code points that are not printable and the grapheme extenders, as Rust 1.98.1 escapes them in the Debug form of a string from its tables of Unicode 17.0.0, enumerated once. The file, not a Unicode version, defines the set. **Unicode pin.** RCE pins Unicode 18.0.0 (https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode18.0.0/) and reads no Unicode table at run time: scalar values and UTF-8 do not change between versions, case and class operations are ASCII, and the two sets of code points a result depends on, White_Space and the display escape set, are enumerated above rather than taken from the toolchain. A newer Rust, Python, JavaScript or JVM therefore cannot change a result; `tests/unicode_pin.rs` checks both sets and scans the runtimes for calls that would read the toolchain's tables, `{:?}` of a text among them, and `tests/emit.rs` compares the display of both ends of every range, and of the code points beside them, on each emitted target with the reference. Moving the pin is a spec change that must leave the enumerated sets unchanged or bump the draft.
rules.N8: Indexing The index `i` of `a[i]` and the ends of `a[i:j]` have type `usize` (W-TY-1 otherwise), so no index is negative. `a[i]` with i ≥ n is `trap("index i out of range")`. A slice end above n is `trap("slice index out of range")`, and i > j is `trap("slice bounds reversed")`; an omitted end is 0 or n. Indexing and slicing are total or trapping by one rule: an out-of-range position is never silently moved.
rules.N9: Limits A list or text built by any operation is at most SIZE_LIMIT = 1,000,000 elements (`trap("size limit")`). A value written to state is at most VALUE_LIMIT = 1,048,576 bytes of canonical JSON (`trap("value limit")`, the state is kept, the value is not recorded).

rules.W-BUD-1: `with budget n` runs the block with a cost budget n: every Form operation charges its cost (C.6.4) and the operation that takes the total past n is `trap("budget")`, at the same operation on every target. The cost table is the reference evaluator's (`interp` and `conc.rs`, `charge`), listed in C.6.4. W-TY-1 if n is not an integer. `with budget n Block else [as e] Else` makes exhaustion a value. Derivation. Totality (T2) asks every step to end in a value; a trap that keeps the state is an outcome of the step, not a value the program can act on. To act on it the program needs a point where the trap is caught, and the state at that point must be one that some sequential execution reaches at a well-defined place, or Else observes a state no specification of Block describes. The only such states are the entry of Block and its completion; the trap rules out completion, so a caught trap restores the entry state. Block is therefore atomic: all of its writes or none (the same law as T30 for `atomic`). Normative rules: - A `trap("budget")` raised while Block runs, by this budget or any enclosing one, is caught by the innermost enclosing budget that has an `else`. Every write Block made (locals, struct fields, state fields, `self`) is undone, then Else runs. - `as e` binds `e: Exhausted`, the builtin `struct Exhausted { limit: u64, used: u64 }`, where `limit` is n and `used` is the units this frame had spent before the operation that would have passed a limit. - Charges stay. Cost counts operations performed (C.6.1), so the units spent in Block remain on every enclosing budget. When the trap came from an outer budget, Else charges that budget, its next charge traps again, and the trap reaches the next budget out with an `else`, or keeps the state. - W-BUD-1: Block of a budget with an `else` holds an effect that a trap cannot undo (`emit`, channel operations, spawn, select, yield, lvar `put` or `freeze`), or returns, breaks or continues out of it. - A budget without `else` behaves as before: the trap keeps the state. - The charge rule: a charge is all or nothing, leaves no frame past its limit, and is additive. Every runtime's `charge` implements the same rule; in this repository the link between those copies is the differential tests, not a proof. The trap falls on the same operation on every target, so whether Else runs, and the value of `e`, are functions of the program and its inputs, and replay re-derives them. The emitters save every local the block writes at entry (struct fields and state fields are locals of the emitted step) and restore them on the trap. Checked by `spec/checker/tests/conc06_run.rs` (`budget_else_catches`, `budget_else_with_undoable_effects_requires_change`), `emit_run.rs` (`budget_else_*`, reference against the Rust, Python and JavaScript runtimes) and `emit06b.rs` (`budget_else_is_atomic_on_every_target`, the limit swept across the block's cost on all four targets).
rules.W-CRDT-1: C.11.5 Merge. `impl Merge for T` declares a join. Its laws (associative, commutative, idempotent) are an admission obligation (W-CRDT-1, `conc::crdt_gate`), discharged by a certificate and never by sampling. `bottom()` is the initial state; the states an LVar can reach are the up-set of it, which the join preserves, so the laws on that up-set are the laws of the type. For a kind of nullary variants the gate evaluates every triple, which decides them (`MergeLaws.laws_of_enum`). Otherwise the gate reads the body of `merge` as a term over proven combinators (`conc::merge_certs`): per field, `max` or `min` on an integer, `or` or `and` on a bool, `union` or `inter` on a `Set[τ]`, `merge` on a `Map[k, v]` (pointwise, certified when the `Merge` of `v` is: an integer, a bool, a set, a map of such, or a type with a certified impl), or `.merge` of a field whose type has a certified impl (componentwise product); on a record of one integer field, a selection that keeps `o` when `o.k > self.k` and `self` otherwise (max, or min when the smaller side is kept); and lexicographic on an integer key: `self` when `self.k > o.k`, `o` when `o.k > self.k`, and otherwise the key with the other fields merged by the rules above. On a tree, if every channel's two ends are compatible, either every process has finished or some channel has both ends waiting on it and they can step (T28d). rules.W-TY-1: if n is not an integer. `with budget n Block else [as e] Else` makes exhaustion a value. Derivation. Totality (T2) asks every step to end in a value; a trap that keeps the state is an outcome of the step, not a value the program can act on. To act on it the program needs a point where the trap is caught, and the state at that point must be one that some sequential execution reaches at a well-defined place, or Else observes a state no specification of Block describes. The only such states are the entry of Block and its completion; the trap rules out completion, so a caught trap restores the entry state. Block is therefore atomic: all of its writes or none (the same law as T30 for `atomic`). Normative rules: - A `trap("budget")` raised while Block runs, by this budget or any enclosing one, is caught by the innermost enclosing budget that has an `else`. Every write Block made (locals, struct fields, state fields, `self`) is undone, then Else runs. - `as e` binds `e: Exhausted`, the builtin `struct Exhausted { limit: u64, used: u64 }`, where `limit` is n and `used` is the units this frame had spent before the operation that would have passed a limit. - Charges stay. Cost counts operations performed (C.6.1), so the units spent in Block remain on every enclosing budget. When the trap came from an outer budget, Else charges that budget, its next charge traps again, and the trap reaches the next budget out with an `else`, or keeps the state. - W-BUD-1: Block of a budget with an `else` holds an effect that a trap cannot undo (`emit`, channel operations, spawn, select, yield, lvar `put` or `freeze`), or returns, breaks or continues out of it. - A budget without `else` behaves as before: the trap keeps the state. - The charge rule: a charge is all or nothing, leaves no frame past its limit, and is additive. Every runtime's `charge` implements the same rule; in this repository the link between those copies is the differential tests, not a proof. The trap falls on the same operation on every target, so whether Else runs, and the value of `e`, are functions of the program and its inputs, and replay re-derives them. The emitters save every local the block writes at entry (struct fields and state fields are locals of the emitted step) and restore them on the trap. rules.W-BUD-1: a call to a `model` foreign function outside `with budget` requires change. The budget is charged at one rule granularity per call (C.6): an emitter counts the same units as the evaluator, so `trap("budget")` falls on the same operation on every target (10.5).
rules.W-CAP-1: Attenuation only narrows: `c.narrow(sub)` returns a `Cap[A]` whose `root` is a path extension of c's. There is no operation that widens. A closure that captures a `Cap[A]`, `&World` or any value of a non-public label requires change (W-CAP-1 extended; F.8, closures): authority held by a closure must be visible in its capture list.
rules.W-CAP-3: a foreign function (5.11) that reads or writes a path takes a `Cap[DirRead]` or `Cap[DirWrite]` parameter after its `&World`. `DirRead` and `DirWrite` are declared authority structs with a `root: text` field. The host checks at the call that the path is under `root` after normalizing it (the normalization is part of the capability's contract, stated in the manifest, F.5.3); the capability's value is logged with the call (5.11), so replay does not re-check it.
rules.W-CAP-4: (caretaker): a `Cap[A]` that is handed to another component is handed as a *caretaker*, a handle the granter keeps and can revoke with a logged event `host.revoke(id)`. A revoke is an entry of the log like any other, so whether a use is before or after a revoke is a function of the log order and replay is exact (T3).
rules.W-CAP-5: a use of a revoked caretaker keeps the state, with the fixed record `{kind: "capability", reason: "revoked", id: ...}`; revoking twice is a no-op entry; a revoked caretaker is never valid again (there is no un-revoke).
rules.W-CON-1: A contract with no satisfying value is an error: under W-CON-1 a function requires change when its `requires` clauses are, in the decidable fragment of W-REF-1, false for every argument. Outside that fragment nothing is decided statically (Q33); the enforcement makes every call of such a function trap, keeping the state, and never succeed vacuously.
rules.W-CON-2: P2 contracts and P3 `ghost` (F.6.2, F.6.3, `tier3.rs`): `requires E` and `ensures E` are statements (`ContractStmt`) written before the first statement of a fn body, after any `ghost let`; a clause elsewhere requires change (W-CON-2). Clauses are enforced always: the checker lowers the fn to guards, `requires` first in written order, then the kept ghost lets, then the body in which every `return` (and the tail value) first binds `result` and runs the `ensures` guards. A violated guard traps with the text `{"clause":"requires"|"ensures","function":"<definition hash>","index":N, "kind":"contract"}` (keys in that sorted order, no spaces), where N counts all the clauses of the fn in written order from 0 and the hash is the definition hash of the fn as written (F.4.3: for a top-level fn the `rce hash` value, for a method the SHA-256 of its canonical text under the same prefix). There is no source span. Under W-CON-1, `requires` clauses that are false in the fragment of literal comparisons, `and` and the integer bounds of one name (`x > 5 and x < 3`) require change; under W-CON-2, `result` in `requires`, a binding named `result` in a fn with `ensures`, and a channel receive in a clause require change. `ghost let` and `ghost fn`: under W-GHOST-1, a ghost name in code that runs requires change; ghost code that no clause names (transitively) is erased, the rest is evaluated because an enforced clause needs it. The emitters do not print a module with a contract (W-RES-1). Not implemented: `ghost` parameters (W-RES-1), `mathint` and quantifiers, `R.check`, opaque types with invariants, assuming a callee's `ensures` and proving its `requires` statically (a call is checked by the enforcement), contracts on function values. T46 and T49 stay unproved.
rules.W-CTFN-1: in a `ct fn`, a value whose label contains `secret` (F.4.2) may not decide an `if`, `match` or `and`/`or` operand, an index, a loop bound, a shift amount, a divisor, or the argument of a call to a function that is not itself `ct`. The branchless `ct_choose(c, a, b)` and the bitwise and arithmetic operators on fixed-width integers (with the usual trap rules) are allowed. Operations that can trap on a secret already require change under W-IFC-4.
rules.W-CTFN-2: an emitter whose target cannot give constant-time guarantees (Python, JavaScript) does not print a `ct fn`; it gives the fixed message "ct fn is not emitted for this target"; the reference evaluator runs it with its ordinary semantics, since time is not observable there. Whether a target does give the guarantee is stated per target in 10.5, not assumed.
rules.W-CTX-1: W-CTX-2: every text parameter of an `extern "model" fn` has the type `&Text[Prompt]`; `&text`, `&[scalar]` and `&mut [scalar]` require change there, and the other parameters are `bool`, an integer or `f64` (5.11). A `Text[Prompt]` is made only by `Prompt.lit` of a literal, `Prompt.encode` and `+` of two of them (W-CTX-1), so the instruction text of every request comes from the program and all data sits in encoded blocks. An argument labeled `untrusted` (F.4.2) requires change unless it is passed as the `&Text[Prompt]` parameter. At run time a `Text[Prompt]` is its text, so the call convention of 5.11 is unchanged.
rules.W-CTX-2: every text parameter of an `extern "model" fn` has the type `&Text[Prompt]`; `&text`, `&[scalar]` and `&mut [scalar]` require change there, and the other parameters are `bool`, an integer or `f64` (5.11). rules.W-CTX-3: a model call is not control dependent on `untrusted` data, and no argument was steered by it outside a `Prompt.encode` block. Requires change: a call in a control context labeled `untrusted` (an `if`, `match`, `while`, `for` or `and`/`or` decided by such a value); a call after a `return`, `break`, `continue`, `fail` or `?` taken under such a condition in the same function, and, for a loop, every call in its body; a `Text[Prompt]` argument whose `untrusted` part did not come only from `Prompt.encode` (for example one chosen by an untrusted branch). With W-CTX-2, untrusted data reaches a model only inside a block made by `Prompt.encode`: it decides neither which instructions are sent nor whether a request is made, unless a step that holds the capability of `label untrusted by A` endorses it first (W-IFC-5). Like W-IFC-2 the rule is termination insensitive: a trap or exhausted fuel ends the run, and the end is logged (C.5). It runs in the label analysis, so only in a module that writes a label (F.12).
rules.W-DEC-1: every call to a function of the same group, from any path, passes a tuple strictly smaller in the lexicographic order than the caller's entry tuple. A group's measure is one tuple for the whole group (Q2); a tail call does not waive the check.
rules.W-DROP-1: an expression statement whose value is not `()` requires change, except a call whose result type is declared `()`. (Under 5.2, discarding an error union already requires change; this extends it to every non-unit value.) To drop on purpose, bind to `_`: `let _ = f(x)`.
rules.W-FFI-1: W-IFC-7: a field of an `extern "model" event` and the result of an `extern "model" fn` are `untrusted`: a label set written on one must name `untrusted`, so `T @ {}` cannot endorse a model answer by declaration. An `extern "model" event` has no field whose type contains `Cap` or `Guarded`. Only the ABI `model` declares an event (W-FFI-1).
rules.W-GHOST-1: a ghost value may not flow into a non-ghost place, into an `emit`, a send, a branch condition of real code, a loop bound or an index. Ghost code is erased before evaluation, emission and hashing of the *run* (it is hashed in the definition, F.4.3). Ghost code is total (F.6.4) and pure.
rules.W-IFC-1: a flow to a place of lower label (an assignment, a call argument, a return, a field, an `emit` field, a send) requires change. An `emit` field and a channel have the public label unless declared `@ {...}`.
rules.W-IFC-2: implicit flows. The label of the control context (the join of the labels of the conditions of every enclosing `if`, `match`, `while`, `for` and guard) joins into every value assigned and every `emit` or send made in it. A loop bound whose label is not public requires change (the number of iterations is observable).
rules.W-IFC-3: provenance. A label name records the input it came from (the event field or foreign result that introduced it); the diagnostic of a flow that requires change names the origin and the sink. Provenance is a property of the checker's report, not of the value, so it never changes a run.
rules.W-IFC-4: kept-outcome channel. A trap or `fail` is itself observable (the kept outcome and its text are an output, 6.1). So a trap site whose deciding operands (a divisor, an index, an operand of an overflowing operation, a size) or whose control context have a non-public label requires change unless the operation is a checked form that returns `Option`, whose label is the join of its operands. The kept-outcome text of a trap or `fail` carries the join of the labels of the operands that decide it; a `fail` payload with a non-public label requires change if the function can return it to a public context.
rules.W-IFC-5: robust declassification. `release e` (the only way to lower a label) is allowed only in a function that holds a `Cap[A]` (5.16) whose authority struct names the label, and only when the control context and the operands that decide whether to release have *trusted* integrity. Integrity is a second set, `{untrusted}`, carried the same way: event payload fields are `untrusted` unless declared otherwise, and `endorse e` (requires a `Cap[A]` that names it) is the only way to make a value trusted. A release decided by untrusted data requires change, so an attacker cannot steer what is released.
rules.W-IFC-6: Information-flow labels (F.4.2, S1): `T @ {A, B}` label sets on declared types (parameters, returns, fields, `let`, `var`), `label NAME [by AUTH]` declarations (W-IFC-6 for an undeclared label), label propagation with the control-flow label (implicit flows), W-IFC-1 (a labeled value reaches a public sink: `emit`, `send`, a store into a public place, a call result), W-IFC-2 (a labeled value decides a loop count), W-IFC-4 (an operation that can trap, and a `fail`, whose deciding operand or control context is labeled), W-IFC-5 (`release` needs the held `Cap[AUTH]` and a trusted deciding context, and `endorse` needs `label untrusted by AUTH` and the held capability; event payloads are `untrusted` unless declared `@ {}`), with the source of each label named in the message and a per-instantiation check of calls. Under W-NAME-2, `label`, `release` and `endorse` used as names require change. The checker erases the labels, `release` and `endorse` before evaluation and emission, so a labeled program runs as the unlabeled one. `declassify` stays reserved, not implemented. The grammar delta is F.13; the Rust LALR(1) tables (0 conflicts), the tree-sitter grammar and its scanner, `parser.c` and the wasm are regenerated from it.
rules.W-IFC-7: a field of an `extern "model" event` and the result of an `extern "model" fn` are `untrusted`: a label set written on one must name `untrusted`, so `T @ {}` cannot endorse a model answer by declaration. An `extern "model" event` has no field whose type contains `Cap` or `Guarded`. Only the ABI `model` declares an event (W-FFI-1).
rules.W-IFLET-1: and the checks of `match` apply. A chain with a second `let` is reserved, not implemented.
rules.W-LAW-1: admission (6.9) evaluates every law of every impl on a fixed, deterministic sample: the values of the impl type that appear in `example`s and `check`s of the program, the boundary values of its fields (zero, one, the extremes of the range, empty, a singleton), and their pairs and triples up to 64 tuples in canonical order. A law that fails on any requires change.
rules.W-LEN-1: S3 typed output (F.5.2, F.5.7): the contexts `ShellArg`, `Prompt` and `Header` (with `lit` and `encode`; the `Prompt` delimiter is `data-` and the SHA-256 of the field, re-hashed until the field does not contain it; `Header.encode` traps on CR and LF) and `Shell`, made only by `Shell.cmd(program, args)` with a literal program and `List[Text[ShellArg]]` arguments, whose value is the canonical JSON `{"args": [...], "program": ...}` (an argument vector, never a command line). `len_bytes` and `len_chars` exist and `len` on text is W-LEN-1. Strict parsing, versioned migrations and the refined-type constructor `R.check` are not implemented. The templates `Prompt.t"..."` of F.6.1 are not implemented either (see below).
rules.W-LEX-4: a source text containing a bidirectional control character (U+202A to U+202E, U+2066 to U+2069), a zero-width or invisible format character (U+200B to U+200F, U+2060, U+FEFF after the first position) or a Unicode scalar value that is not assigned in the pinned Unicode version (6.3 N7) inside a string or comment requires change. A string that needs one of these writes it with `\u{...}`. Identifiers are ASCII (2.3), so look-alike names cannot occur. The reference checker also reports as requiring change, in a string or comment, the C0 and C1 controls other than the line feed, the other invisible or blank-looking format characters (U+00AD, U+034F, U+061C, U+115F, U+1160, U+17B4, U+17B5, U+180E, U+2061 to U+2064, U+3164, U+FFA0, U+FFF9 to U+FFFB), the tag block (U+E0000 to U+E007F) and Unicode noncharacters; for "unassigned" it reports planes 4 to 13 and the noncharacters only, because no general-category table is vendored (F.12).
rules.W-MATCH-2: W-UNUSED-2: a `match` arm that cannot be reached (W-MATCH-2 already) and an `if`, `elif`, `while` or guard whose condition is a comptime constant (9.8, Q17) require change.
rules.W-MOD-2: W-PIN-1: a module whose hash differs from its manifest entry, a dependency that is not pinned by hash, an import that is a glob or relative path, and an import cycle (W-MOD-2) require change. Imports are an unordered set; adding an export is always compatible. There is no resolver: the manifest is the whole answer.

Under W-NAME-2, only shadowing of a parameter, field or module-level name required change; this extends it to every enclosing local.

rules.W-RES-1: Under W-RES-1, the reserved words `declassify` and `law` and the type names `Template` and `mathint` require change (their constructs are not implemented), except directly after `.`; the `# rce-version:` label is ignored (2.7).
rules.W-TPL-1: a `Template` plus text, or a template used as text, requires change. A template is made into text only by a renderer: `C.t"..."` for a context C (F.5.2) renders each field through `C.encode`; `text.t"..."` renders each field through `tostr`, and a field type that is not text must implement `Show` (5.9; Q18). There is no implicit locale and no implicit display.
rules.W-TPL-2: P6 templates (F.6.1): `TEMPLATE` is a token (F.13). Only the two rendered forms are implemented: `text.t"..."` and `C.t"..."` for `Html`, `Url`, `Sql`, `Json`, `ShellArg` and `Prompt`. The parser expands them at once to the concatenation they mean (`text`: literal segments and `f.tostr()` of each field; a context: `C.lit` of each segment and `C.encode` of each field, joined with `+`), so the fields are ordinary reads and the context's typing (W-CTX-1) decides what a field may be. Fields are an identifier or a field path; `{{` and `}}` are literal braces; an empty field, an expression, a stray brace and an unclosed field require change (W-TPL-2); so does a renderer that is neither `text` nor a context (W-TPL-1). A template that is not rendered at once is the `Template[τ]` value of F.6.1, which requires change as reserved, not implemented (W-RES-1), so W-TPL-1's text-plus-template cases cannot arise yet. The formatter writes the expansion, not the template (the meaning, and so the hash of the expansion, is the same). T44 stays unproved.
rules.W-TRI-1: (static): a program that has `private` and `untrusted` inputs and an external sink with no `release` path that satisfies W-IFC-5 requires change; the rule is a consequence of W-IFC-1 and is stated so the broker and the checker agree. The checker enforces it by W-IFC-1 (a labeled value reaching an `emit`, a send, a foreign argument or a public store) and W-IFC-5 (a `release` needs a held capability and a trusted deciding context), with no separate check: a separate check would also require change in programs in which the private value never reaches the sink, which W-IFC-1 admits. A model answer is an `untrusted` input by W-IFC-7 (F.5.6).
rules.W-TX-1: a function body in which a non-undoable effect can happen before a `fail` on some path (a path from a non-undoable effect to a `fail`, or to a call of a function that may `fail`) requires change. So a function that performs I/O does not also fail after it; it returns a `Result` value (F.8) the caller examines. (Q1.)
rules.W-TY-2: Strict positivity holds without a rule: a recursive `kind` mentions itself only as a direct field, because a `fn` type cannot occur inside a data type (W-TY-2) (Q23).
rules.W-UNUSED-1: a `let`, `var`, parameter, pattern binding or `use` name that is never read requires change. The wildcard `_` and any name beginning with `_` are exempt as the one spelling for "deliberately unused"; a name beginning with `_` that is read also requires change (so the spelling means one thing).
rules.W-UNUSED-2: a `match` arm that cannot be reached (W-MATCH-2 already) and an `if`, `elif`, `while` or guard whose condition is a comptime constant (9.8, Q17) require change.
rules.W-WORLD-1: an `extern` declaration (5.11) has `&World` as its first parameter; a call to a foreign function passes a `&World` that the caller itself holds; `fn main` and task functions may declare a `&World` parameter, and no other context may (a pure function, a step or a handler holds none, as 5.2 already forbids the call). A foreign function declared without it is W-WORLD-1.
